# Exercise 2

<!-- How many observations and variables are in the data? Use code to support you answer. -->

<!-- Why is it important to answer these questions before beginning an analysis? -->
 + There are 30 rows, which represent observations. There are 4 coulmns, which represent variables.
+ A single row represents a patient.
+ R interpreted the `gender_code` and `baseline_score` as characters even though their non-missing values are numerical codes and scores. This occurred because their missing values are represented with characters.

# Exercise 3
<!-- Import patients.csv again and assign the result to an object named patients. -->

<!-- This time, use the na argument in read_csv() to identify "Not recorded" and "." as missing values. -->

<!-- Use glimpse() and summary() to inspect patients, and then respond to the following: -->

<!--     Which variables changed type and why? -->
<!--     Did identifying the missing values change the number of rows or columns? Why or why not? -->
<!--     Although gender_code is now stored as a numerical variable, should it be interpreted as a quantitative measurement? Explain. -->
<!--     What does this example demonstrate about the difference between a variable’s storage type and its meaning? -->
+ `gender_code` and `baseline_code` changed type because we've told R to identify its two character values as NA.
+ It didn't change the number rows and columns. Change in type does not reduce or add number of observations and variables.
+ `gender_code` is a qualitative measurement. Even though it's numerical, they're discrete values that alternate between `1`'s and `0`'s.
+ A variables being a numeric values doesn't necesarily mean that it represents a quantitative value. 

```{r ex-3}
patients <- read_csv("data/patients.csv",na = c("Not recorded","."))
glimpse(patients)
summary(patients)

```

# Exercise 4
+ `score_change` contains a missing value because the `baseline_score` for
patient `P017` is missing. It does not represent an unchanged score.
+ There was an increase in health-awareness scores for most patients. Three patients
saw their scores decline however.
```{r}
score_change <- c(patients$followup_score - patients$baseline_score)
t.test(score_change, mu = 0) 
#Consulted Claude Opus 4.8 for assistance for above t test. 
#Chat can be accessed here: https://claude.ai/share/8623d47a-8c3b-4890-8731-b758ca210aa2
```

$H_0: \mu_{diff} = 0$

$H_A: \mu_{diff} \neq 0$

$\alpha = 0.01$

We can reject $H_0$. The program caused the observed changes as per the `t test`



```{r ex-4}

# patients <- read_csv("data/patients.csv",na = c("Not recorded","."))
score_change <- c(patients$followup_score - patients$baseline_score)

print(score_change)
print(score_change[5])
class(score_change)
summary(score_change)
print(mean(score_change,na.rm = TRUE))
print(median(score_change, na.rm = TRUE))
print(min(score_change, na.rm = TRUE))
print(max(score_change, na.rm = TRUE))
sum(score_change < 0, na.rm = TRUE) # number of patients with declined scores

```

# Exercise 5

```{r ex-5}

print(dim(patients) == dim(patients_check))
glimpse(patients_check)


```
+ Checking an exported file by importing and verifying it enables us to analyse
the same data across different devices without hiccups like making sure it's in the right
location.
  

# Exercise 6
<!-- What is the relationship between flipper length and body mass in penguins from the Palmer Archipelago in Antartica? -->

<!-- Construct a scatterplot with: -->

<!--     flipper_length_mm on the x-axis; and -->
<!--     body_mass_g on the y-axis. -->

<!-- Include an informative title and descriptive axis labels with the units of measurement. -->

<!-- Finally, respond to the following: -->

<!--     What relationship do you observe between flipper length and body mass? -->
<!--     Did R produce a warning? If so, what does it mean? -->


```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
glimpse(penguins)

ggplot(data = penguins, 
       mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Flipper length and body mass",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Penguins from Palmer Archipelago",
       x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)")

```
+ There is a positive linear relationship between Body mass and Flipper length.
+ R produced a warning. It alerts that 2 rows containing missing values or outside
the scale range were removed.


# Exercise 7
<!-- Modify your plot from Exercise 6 so that dot color represents penguin species. -->

<!-- Then, respond to the following: -->

<!--     What additional information does color reveal? -->
<!--     Does the overall relationship appear to be explained partly by differences among species? Explain using evidence from the visualization. -->
<!--     In your code, was color mapped to a variable or set to a constant value? How do you know? -->

```{r}
penguin_data <- penguins
species_factor <- factor(penguins$species)
ggplot(data = penguins, 
       mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Flipper length and body mass",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Penguins from Palmer Archipelago",
       x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", color = "Species")

```
+ The color reveals that Gentoo penguins are have overall higher body mass and 
flipper length than Adelle and Chinstrap penguins.
+ Yes, the overall the relationship between the two variables is made more pronounced
with the addition of gentoo penguins
+ color is mapped to a variable. The mapping is inside `aes`.

# Exercise 8
<!-- Create another version of the scatterplot that uses separate facets for the three penguin species instead of mapping species to color. -->

<!-- Compare the faceted plot with the color-coded plot from Exercise 7. -->

<!--     What is easier to see in the color-coded plot? -->
<!--     What is easier to see in the faceted plot? -->
<!--     Which version would you use to communicate the relationship among species, flipper length, and body mass? Briefly justify your choice based on your communication goal. -->


```{r}

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(species ~ island) 
```
+ It's easier to see the overall relationship between the two variables on the color
coded plot
+ It's easier to see the relationship between flipper length and body mass within a species
+ I'd use the color-coded plot. If my goal is to communicate the relationship between all three variables, the color-coded one does a better job at displaying a more linear relationship and isn't specific to one species.

# Exercise 9

+ I predicted a scatterplot identical to the one above with the added difference of
color set to `navyblue`. 

+ `navyblue` is being read as a category with the same value for each row. Therefore,
there's a legend with a single entry.

+ The points aren't navy blue because `navyblue` was specified inside `aes`
which makes R think that it's mapped to data and not a color setting.

+ Placing color, alpha and size inside or outside `aes()` is what determines whether
they're determined by a variable inside the data or not. For example, if `color` 
is inside `aes`, each category inside the specified column will get a color. If placed 
inside `geom_point`, then it will not be mapped to the column.


```{r}
ggplot(
  penguins,
  aes(
    x = flipper_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    
  )
) +
  geom_point(color = "navyblue", alpha=0.5, size = 5)

```
